reason: Attacked as a likely Victorian anthology drift and it survived. The Bibelot, Volume I, Number V, fetched this run, reprints Wharton’s page of selected renderings for this fragment and prints the Symonds version as ‘Evening, all things thou bringest / Which dawn spread apart from each other; / The lamb and the kid thou bringest, / Thou bringest the boy to his mother.’ — verbatim with the proposed quotation, credited to J. A. Symonds, 1883, and set beside Wharton’s own literal prose (‘Evening, thou that bringest all that bright morning scattered…’), Edwin Arnold’s 1869 quatrain, Byron’s imitation in Don Juan iii.107 and Tennyson’s in Leonine Elegiacs. A second search returned the same four lines with the same attribution. The obvious failure mode here is quoting Wharton’s literal prose or Arnold under Symonds’ name; the entry does neither, and it does not run the verse together as prose. Numbering: Wharton’s fragment 95 is Lobel and Page 104a, so the locator is right in both systems, though the source line gives only the modern number while naming Wharton’s edition, which is a small mismatch worth tidying. Attribution: Sappho’s, no speaker question, no entry on the misattribution list. Cap and ban: shipped.js returns sappho, yearCount 0, atCap false, banned false, shipped [], near []. Scope and form: ancient text in an 1883 published translation, both pre-2000; publishable; the source line leads with the name, carries no dash, runs 94 characters, the quotation ends in a full stop and uses curly apostrophes; tag Poetry is the form of the work. Nit only: the Bibelot indents lines 2 and 4, which the slash convention does not record and does not need to.
